The bank_source default is 'slot' (L95), and the docstring says that source holds 5 old classes. prep_geo2 really does skip glued per geometry ('no family FULL parent' L288, 'no glue face with material' L294) and support_k (L446), so even a correct bank_source='data' run renormalises per geometry. HostBanks.clean can also remove classes. The current four arms (5 old classes, slot) are not affected. The full-data v2 run now being prepared is exactly where this bites silently.

items.title: The selection criterion depends on each arm's mix and bank source, so cross-arm best.pt choices are not comparable
items.claim: By default score_classes = the non-adv mix classes with w > 0. Arms with different mixes (control vs new-data arms) therefore pick best.pt by different criteria. score/families also average each class only over the geometries that have it, so a class skipped or removed per geometry changes the family mean. The val banks also differ by bank source: the slot cache holds the NaN-cleaned old support banks (58/8/8 samples on 5 geometries), while the data dir after prep_geo2 --fix-support holds recomputed support banks.
items.evidence: train3.py:584 `score_classes = cfg.get('score_classes') or [c for c, w in mix.items() if c != 'adv' and w > 0]`. families() L341 `rs = [per_geo[case][c] for case in cases if c in per_geo[case]]`. score() L360-362 average over `c in d`. prep_geo2 docstring: '--fix-support recompute the old support class ... old files kept as *.nan_bak.npy'. The r2 pilot deliberately selected on the '5 个基础类' (5 base classes).
items.consequence: In v2 full-data arm comparisons, best.pt for a new-data arm can be selected partly on force_c/glued/support_k, while the control is selected on the old classes. The support-class val means also differ in content whenever a fixed geometry is in val. Both bias the v2 data decision.
items.fix: For every comparison arm, set score_classes explicitly to the 5 base classes (report new classes separately). Evaluate every arm on the same val bank source (data dir), or log which bank source and val sample counts entered each class mean. Consider adding a strict per-family completeness check to score().

verification.reasoning: L584 sets the default score_classes from the arm's own mix. families() (L341) and score() (L360-362) average only over the geometries and classes present. So arms with different mixes select on different criteria. The default is documented (docstring L42), and it is a config-level fix; the r2 pilot already used explicit 5-base-class selection via train1. The current four arms share mix and bank_source='slot', so their criteria match. The bank-source point also holds. Slot banks are the cleaned NaN-laden old support banks, while --fix-support recomputes them in the data dir, so val content differs between sources. This matters only for future data arms, so I downgraded it to minor.

items.title: quota_counts under-samples small-weight classes (without-replacement draw is not inclusion-proportional)
items.claim: The remainder is drawn without replacement with draw probabilities fr/sum(fr). The resulting inclusion probabilities are not fr, so the expected counts differ from w_c*B.
items.evidence: trainlib.py:334 `n[gen.choice(len(x), size=r, replace=False, p=fr / fr.sum())] += 1`. A local 40k-batch simulation (B=16) gave: for mix .3/.2/.3/.2, expected counts 4.753/3.249 vs 4.8/3.2 (-1%/+1.5%). For a 9-class v2-like mix with two 0.05 classes, 0.706/0.711 vs 0.8 (-12%), while 0.15 classes were +2.4%. The unit test's 0.08 tolerance (t_train3 t_quota) hides this.
items.consequence: With the larger v2 mixes, rare classes get about 10% less exposure than configured. This matters for the plan to hold the face-class share.
items.fix: Use systematic (Madow) sampling of the remainder: u ~ U(0,1), give +1 to class i when the cumulative fr crosses u + j for an integer j. Inclusion probabilities are then exactly fr_i and the draw is still seeded.

verification.reasoning: I reproduced the simulation locally on CPU with 40k batches, B=16. For .3/.2/.3/.2 the expected counts were 4.753/3.249/4.755/3.242 against 4.8/3.2. For a 9-class mix with two 0.05 classes they were 0.707/0.703 against 0.8 (-12%), while the 0.15 classes were +2%. With the arms' actual mix (quota=True) macro 0.1 came out -2.9%. The docstring describes the draw correctly, but the realised class shares differ from the mix. The effect is small for current mixes and larger for mixes with rare classes.

items.title: Adversarial buffer is never refreshed without F; first-visit vectors are only approximately at unit exact energy
items.claim: On later visits, rescore() runs, but when the geometry has no F banks (bank_source 'slot', or data without --F-old for the classes used) advbuf[case] is left unchanged. The directions stay those from the first visit, possibly found with a very early model. When F exists, first-visit vectors, normalised through the fp32 Neumann factor, are ranked by e_hat against bank-Ritz vectors whose unit exact energy is exact.
items.evidence: L509-525: only the `if fcl and A['R'] > 0:` branch reassigns advbuf[case]; otherwise it only logs buffer_top. Geo.adversarial L233 builds G = X^T Y on the assumption that S X = Y, which holds only as far as the fp32 Neumann solve does, so the exact energy of X is 1 + O(factor error). rescore L489 uses e_hat (= Rayleigh quotient only at unit exact energy).
items.consequence: In slot-source runs longer than about one pass over the training set, the 'adv' mix share trains on stale directions. This differs from train2's fresh search per entry, and the train3 docstring only half says so. Buffer ranking is slightly inconsistent between the two vector origins.
items.fix: Without F, either re-run the fp32 power iteration every N-th visit (warm-started from the buffer) or log ADV_STALE and treat the adv weight as a known difference. Store the exact-energy estimate of the first-visit vectors, or renormalise them, before ranking them against bank-Ritz vectors.

verification.reasoning: In adv_entry, advbuf[case] is reassigned on a later visit only inside `if fcl and A['R'] > 0` (L513-523). Otherwise rescore is computed but used only for the buffer_top log. All four arms use bank_source='slot', which has no F, so their buffers are never refreshed. In practice the effect is small there: 15k steps with swap_every 100 gives about 150 entries over 148 training geometries, so there are almost no later visits. It grows in longer runs. The docstring says refresh needs F. First-visit X is S-normalised through G = X^T P Y, which assumes S X = P Y from the fp32 Neumann solve. So its exact energy is 1+O(factor error), and ranking it by e_hat against the exactly normalised bank-Ritz vectors is slightly inconsistent, as the finding says.

items.title: Resume does not reproduce the uninterrupted run, and best.pt/EMA can be wrong after resume
items.claim: Resume reseeds gen/agen/ogen from the step instead of restoring their states, drops adversarial buffers, double-counts visits for the rebuilt pool, and restores `best` from ckpt.pt, which can be older than the latest best.pt. If the checkpoint has no 'ema', the EMA silently keeps the init weights rather than the resumed weights.
items.evidence: L564-565 `gen = np.random.default_rng([seed, ck['step']])` etc. The ckpt dict at L740 holds no generator states and no advbuf. admit L545-546 increments visits n for pool members already counted in the restored visits. best comes from ckpt (L560), but best.pt is written at every eval (L736-738) between checkpoints, so after a resume a later eval with a score between the two values overwrites a better best.pt. The EMA is built at L447 before the resume load and only loaded `if ck.get('ema') is not None` (L561).
items.consequence: A resumed arm differs from an uninterrupted one in data order, views and adversarial state, which confounds small arm differences. best.pt can silently end up worse than a previously saved best, and visit statistics are inflated.
items.fix: Save gen/agen/ogen bit_generator.state and tgen.get_state() in ckpt.pt, plus optionally advbuf (host fp32, a few MB per geometry). On resume, set best = min(ck['best'], score stored in best.pt). If cfg ema > 0 and the checkpoint has no EMA, reset the EMA to the resumed weights and log it. Do not increment visits n during the pool rebuild.

verification.reasoning: On resume, generators are reseeded from the step (L564-565) rather than restored, and ckpt (L740) has no RNG state and no advbuf. The pool rebuild (L567-571) calls admit, which increments visits n (L545-546) for members already counted in the restored visits. best comes from ckpt.pt. With the arms' ckpt_every=2000 and eval_every=5000, an eval such as 5000 can write best.pt before the next ckpt. A crash then replays from the older ckpt with its older best, and the replayed eval, now on a different trajectory, can overwrite best.pt. The EMA is loaded only if the ckpt has one (L561); otherwise it keeps the init weights. That needs an ema=0 run resumed with ema>0, which is an edge case. All of these are real but conditional on resumes.

items.title: Non-reproducibility is not only cuDSS: CUDA atomics in the forward/backward, and ADV_FAIL shifts the batch RNG stream
items.claim: The V2 doc attributes same-seed run-to-run differences to the cuDSS fp32 factor. The model itself uses float index_add_ on CUDA (scatter atomics), and torch.use_deterministic_algorithms is never enabled in the trainers, so training is not bitwise reproducible even with adv_on_load off. The gen stream also depends on whether each geometry has an adv buffer: an OOM-driven ADV_FAIL removes 'adv' from `names`, which changes how many draws each later batch consumes.
items.evidence: models.py:579/583/597/643/648/654 index_add_. trainlib _Sens.backward L69 grad.index_add_. t_evalcost docstring: 'CUDA atomics are not bitwise reproducible'. trainlib.py:459/461 names and multinomial/quota depend on `adv is not None`. train3 L686 passes advbuf.get(s.case).
items.consequence: Deterministic adversarial search alone would not make reruns reproducible, and a single OOM changes all later batches. Arm differences of 1-4% need several seeds, not only a same-config rerun.
items.fix: State the full set of non-determinism sources in the doc. Keep the batch-sampling RNG independent of adv state (a separate generator for adv column indices, with a fixed number of draws per step). Use ≥2 seeds per arm for decisions.

verification.reasoning: With sparse=true, the fine hyperedge layers go through sparse_layers. But geometry() (models.py:579, 583, 597-598), _restrict (648-649) and _prolong (654-655) always use float index_add_ on CUDA, which uses atomics and is non-deterministic. So do the backward passes of the gathers and _Sens.backward. No trainer enables torch.use_deterministic_algorithms. t_evalcost's own docstring says CUDA atomics are not bitwise reproducible, while the V2 doc (section 1, note) names only cuDSS. An ADV_FAIL leaves advbuf without the case, so `names` in sample() drops 'adv'. That changes the multinomial/quota categories and the number of gen draws, shifting every later batch.

items.title: Default val_max=8 truncates the family-ordered val list to 1-2 of the 4 val families
items.claim: make_split writes val as the concatenation of whole families. `split['val'][:val_max]` with the default 8 therefore covers only the first family or two, and score() then averages only over the families present, even though the docstring describes a 4-family decision rule.
items.evidence: train3.py:423 `val_cases = split['val'][:cfg.get('val_max', 8)]`. make_split.py `val=[g for f in val_f for g in sorted(fam[f])]`. score() L356 `fs = [f for f in (val_families or sorted(fam_agg)) if f in fam_agg]`. eval_views used 20 val geometries.
items.consequence: Any run that relies on the default selects on a subset of families, and mu_cases shrinks the same way. The arm configs could not be checked here.
items.fix: Default val_max to all of val. Log or raise when fewer than all split['val_families'] enter the score.

verification.reasoning: The default really is val_max=8 (L423), and make_split orders val by whole families, so the default truncates to the first families. score() silently uses only the families present (L356). The finding's consequence is limited to runs that rely on the default, though. All four v2 arms (g_cfg.sh) and s2_full set val_max=20, which matches the 20 val geometries eval_views used, so the arms' selection is not affected. This is a latent footgun in the default only.

items.title: The tail term (C3) turns off silently for every batch containing a class without F
items.claim: F is returned only when every non-adv column has reactions. Otherwise batch_loss skips the tail term with no log other than the missing 'tail' key in STEP lines, which are written only every log_every steps.
items.evidence: trainlib.py:479 `if want_F and all(f is not None for f in fc)`. train3.py:222 `if tw > 0 and F is not None`. F for the old classes exists only after prep_geo2 --F-old.
items.consequence: A tail_w>0 arm on a data dir without --F-old reactions is effectively the control for most batches, and the comparison would wrongly conclude that C3 has no effect.
items.fix: When tail_w > 0, raise at load if any mix class lacks F (or log it per geometry), and count tail-active steps in the STEP/EVAL records.

verification.reasoning: trainlib.py:479 returns F only if every non-adv column has F, and batch_loss (L222) skips the tail term when F is None. The only signal is a missing 'tail' key in STEP lines every log_every steps, with no per-geometry log or count. The docstring (L22) states the condition. No current arm uses tail_w (default 0), so this is latent: it matters for a future C3 arm on data without --F-old.

items.title: With oh=true the unused base-geometry model cache stays on the device; pool_dofs does not account for it
items.claim: Pool members train only on the view (tgeo), but Slot keeps and moves both the base cache and the view cache to the device. Model cache memory per pool member roughly doubles, and the DOF cap ignores this.
items.evidence: Slot.__init__ L160-161 model.add_geo(g) (base cache). set_view L172-173 adds the view cache. Slot.to L205-210 re-registers and moves both. Training uses `geo = s.tgeo` (L685) and adv_entry uses s_.tgeo. pool_dofs admission (L542) counts only DOFs.
items.consequence: Extra device memory per pool member (size not measured here), which raises OOM/ADV_FAIL risk for large geometries in O_h runs. ADV_FAIL in turn changes the RNG stream (TRAINER-8).
items.fix: While a view is set, keep the base cache on the host (move it to the device only for evaluation), or rebuild it lazily.

verification.reasoning: Slot.__init__ registers the base cache (L160-161), set_view adds the view cache (L172-173), and Slot.to/_move move and register both (L178-183, L205-210). Training forwards only s.tgeo (the view). The base cache is used only if a pool member is also a probe during eval, and pool members are moved to the host during eval anyway. So an unused MGCache stays on the device, and admission counts DOFs only. The 'roughly doubles' figure is overstated. Sparse patterns are built lazily in _pat only on forward, so the base cache usually lacks them and is smaller than the view cache. The size is unmeasured.

items.title: train1 has no bank cleaning or non-finite guard, and a NaN score freezes best.pt (also possible in train3)
items.claim: train1 samples from uncleaned Geo banks and calls opt.step without an isfinite check, so a NaN bank column poisons the weights. A NaN first score sets best=NaN, and `score < best` is then always False, so best.pt is never updated again. train3 has the same `best is None or sc < best` pattern (L736) when the first score is NaN.
items.evidence: train1.py:65-81 (no isfinite on loss/gn before opt.step); L101 `score = max(v[c]['mean'] ...)` with NaN means; L104 `if best is None or score < best`. train2.clean_banks exists but train1 never calls it. The old support banks are ~89% NaN on 5 geometries.
items.consequence: A train1 fine-tune on one of those geometries, with support in the mix and data without --fix-support, silently diverges or keeps a stale best.pt.
items.fix: Call a cleaning step (HostBanks.clean semantics) in train1, skip non-finite steps as train3 does, and treat a NaN score as +inf in both trainers.

verification.reasoning: train1 builds TL.Geo, which loads the raw data-dir banks and never cleans them. sample_with_sens picks columns uniformly, and the loop calls opt.step after clip_grad_norm_ with no isfinite check. A NaN column gives NaN grads, clip scales them by NaN, and Adam then writes NaN weights. The score is Python max over the class means. It is NaN if the first mean is NaN, and then `score < best` stays False forever, so best.pt is never updated again. The train3 part is much weaker. score() uses _nanmean, which drops non-finite values at every level, so sc is NaN only if every family total is non-finite. train3 also skips non-finite losses and grads. The defect is real mainly for train1 on the NaN-support geometries, run on data without --fix-support.

title: Gate, evaluation and decision integrity
checked_ok: The traction-consistent gate loads are the 6 per config (test and neighbour face on the load plane, x/y/z) with gate=True. The cut-surface traction loads carry gate=False and enter only cut_*_max. evalnet labels 'uniform' rows role='stress'. This matches the standing rule (consistent loads = gate, uniform nodal = stress, both configs x and y, neighbour cell included unless LAT_SKIP_NBR_SENS).

Q2 face-traction weights: at xi=0 or 1 the Lagrange basis reduces to [1,0,0] / [0,0,1], so only face nodes receive load. port_node_ids = nodes[onport] keeps NODES order, so `wv[np.isin(C.nodes, C.port_node_ids)]` lines up with idx rows. The neighbour's local load plane value is 0 in both configs.

Lattice assembly and reference: gluing by absolute node position, private cut-band DOFs, clamping of the far face, and a dense fp64 Cholesky of the exact port operators. PCG with the exact lattice factor as preconditioner gives spectrum >= 1 for an upper-bound operator. Compliance = F^T X, relative error vs reference.

lat_full cell_metrics: eps_c = q^T S_hat q / q^T S q - 1 at the exact lattice port data, w_c = E_c / C, and the bound (C - C_hat)/C <= sum w eps follows from K_hat >= K at V = U. The additivity ratio is computed as described.

eval_views: identity is g.field and rotated is oh.view with the field returned in the original frame, energies with the original K at unit exact energy. 'mean' is the per-view mean over geometries of class means, and 'mean_over_rotated' averages the non-identity views. Views 5, 17, 29, 38 are proper rotations and 46 is improper. val_max=20 covers all 20 val geometries (4 families).

compare_arms per-family ratios, the pooled geometric mean over classes and worst_class_mean_ratio are computed as the docstring describes (apart from the issues listed in the findings). The EMA/raw selection key is read correctly from the EVAL record.

train3 score(): families are weighted equally, classes absent from a family are skipped, and the sensitivity term is added only when finite. Stratified probes are seeded, cover the strata round-robin and terminate. EMA.applied restores the raw weights. best.pt stores the selected (EMA) weights, and those are what evalnet/lat_full load.
The trainlib Geo.evaluate / eval_geo energy excess e_hat - 1 at unit exact energy, the per-sample relative sensitivity error, and s_hat_apply = 0.5·grad(u^T K u) = E_hat^T K E_hat q.

diag_error: Galerkin check err^T K err = e_hat - e (the exact field is K-harmonic in the interior). The ghost share is K minus the body moments part, and assemble() confirms K = GP base + moment element terms.

bench_deploy: the exact and learned per-cell S q timings both use warm=1, reps=3, with synchronisation. The Jacobi preconditioner (diag of the assembled K_PP) is the same for both operators. The exact route includes the fp64 refinement. The lattice neighbour is the family FULL parent (regex).

items.title: The arm decision rule ignores sensitivity, the gate's binding metric
items.claim: compare_arms' 'better' flag depends only on energy-class means: pooled family wins on the family class-mean energy ratio, plus the worst class val_mean energy ratio <= 1.10. Sensitivity ratios (sens_ratio), p90, per-geometry max, mu and cert are computed for the report but never enter the decision.
items.evidence: compare_arms.py:49-51 `ratios = [af[fam][c]['mean'] / bf[fam][c]['mean'] ...]; pooled_wins += int(np.exp(np.mean(np.log(ratios))) < 1)`; line 68 `r['better'] = bool(pooled_wins >= 3 and r['worst_class_mean_ratio'] <= 1.10)`. sens_ratio (line 56) is computed but not used. In every r2 pilot gate row the binding metric is sensitivity, not compliance (p_ctrl 1.24/2.09, p_A y 0.77/2.97, V2 doc section 8). The one arm that failed the gate (p_sl1: sensitivity 2.1% -> 3.8%) failed only on sensitivity. ARCH_REVIEW stage-4 criteria also list per-geometry max/p90, mu and cert flags, and none of them is enforced.
items.consequence: An arm can be declared 'better' while it makes the gate metric worse. The flag is biased exactly along the axis where the new-data arms regressed (gate y load-6 sensitivity 2.06% -> 3.0%).
items.fix: Make 'better' require a sens_ratio no worse than a tolerance (per family, same >= 3/4 rule), plus no regression in geo_max_ratio_median and the mu of the fixed geometries. Better still, add the lattice-gate metrics (lat_full on held-out families) as a hard veto.

verification.reasoning: The code matches the claim. compare_arms.py:68 sets 'better' only from pooled_wins, which comes from class-mean energy ratios (lines 49-51), and from worst_class_mean_ratio. sens_ratio, p90, geo_max_ratio_median, mu and cert are computed but never used in the flag. I downgraded it for three reasons. (1) compare_arms only covers the step-2 'c_' arms (line 34). The r2 pilot arms (p_*) that the evidence cites were judged directly on the evalnet gate (chain3.sh), not by this rule, so the p_sl1 and p_A/p_B examples are not cases of compare_arms mis-deciding. (2) The stage-4 criteria in ARCH_REVIEW (line ~332) are '3 of 4 families' plus 'look at' max/p90/mu/cert, which reads as human review of reported numbers, and they do not list sensitivity. (3) train3's own selection score does include the sensitivity term. Still a real gap: validation sensitivity is measured and then ignored by the flag.

items.title: The '>= 3 of 4 families' rule is a coin-flip test with a 31% false-positive rate, and replicates reuse the same seed
items.claim: A family 'win' is any ratio below 1 with no margin or noise model. If an arm has no effect and the four family signs are independent and symmetric, P(>= 3 wins of 4) = 5/16 ≈ 31%, and the <= 1.10 class clause almost never binds under noise. The review's safeguard ('胜出者用 2 个种子确认') is not implemented. The replicate runs c_ctrl2 / p_ctrl2 copy the control config with the SAME seed (g_q.sh: c['out'] changed only, 'seeds' printed), so they measure cuDSS nondeterminism only, not seed-to-seed variance.
items.evidence: compare_arms.py:51 `int(... < 1)` (no margin). The V2 doc itself says the same-seed single-step loss varies 2-8% between reruns (t_evalcost) while the arm differences are 1-4%. Every arm (c_*, p_*) is a single seed (seed=0 or seed=1). g_q.sh builds c_ctrl2/p_ctrl2 from c_ctrl.json/p_ctrl.json with only 'out' changed.
items.consequence: A neutral arm has roughly a 1-in-3 chance of being called 'better'. With about 10 arms planned, false winners are expected. The noise floor estimated from same-seed reruns underestimates the true variance, so 1-4% differences (B1/B2 'neutral', the new-data regressions) are not statistically established either way.
items.fix: Run at least 2 seeds per arm and per control (different 'seed' values, not just a rerun). Require each family win to exceed the control's seed-to-seed spread (or use a paired sign test over geometries within families with a stated alpha). Report 'undecided' when the margin is inside the noise.

verification.reasoning: compare_arms.py:51 counts a family win as any geometric-mean ratio below 1, with no margin. Under a null of 4 independent, symmetric signs, P(>=3 of 4) = 5/16. g_q.sh builds c_ctrl2 and p_ctrl2 by changing only 'out', so they reuse seed=0 (g_cfg.sh) and seed=1 (g_chain3.sh). They therefore measure only cuDSS/adversarial nondeterminism, not seed-to-seed variance. Every arm config has exactly one seed. The review's own safeguard ('胜出的臂用 2 个种子确认', ARCH_REVIEW stages 3/4 and the statistics note) is not implemented anywhere. The V2 doc itself says 1-4% arm differences need reruns before any conclusion.

items.title: Gate pass/fail is decided at the threshold edge, inside the run-to-run noise
items.claim: gate_pass is a hard `<= 0.03` comparison with no margin and no replicate. The r2 pilot declares p_A (y sensitivity 2.97%) and p_B (3.00%) as passing the gate. Both are single-seed, and both are within 0.03 percentage points of the threshold.
items.evidence: lattice3.py:282 `out['gate_pass'] = bool(ce[g].max() <= 0.03 and np.nanmax(vec[:, g]) <= 0.03)`. V2 doc section 8: p_A '0.77 / 2.97 ✅', p_B '0.91 / 3.00 ✅'. For this same load the control moves 2.06 -> ~3.0 with a data change, and the trainer is not bitwise reproducible.
items.consequence: The ✅ on p_A/p_B, and any v2 claim built on 'the new data keeps the gate', is not reproducible. A rerun can flip it, so recommending a full data re-prep with classes A and B rests on a coin-flip gate outcome.
items.fix: Report the gate with a margin (e.g. pass only if <= 2.7%, 'marginal' between 2.7% and 3.0%). Rerun marginal arms with 2 seeds and gate each checkpoint. Record the gate verdict as a distribution, not as a boolean.

verification.reasoning: lattice3.py:282 is a hard <= 0.03 test with no margin and no replicate, and the section-8 table marks p_A (2.97%) and p_B (3.00%) as passing. Both come from single-seed, non-bitwise-reproducible runs. I downgraded it because the doc does not rest its recommendation on those checkmarks. It explicitly flags the y load-6 rise 2.06% -> ~3.0% as a same-direction regression and asks to watch it in the gate. The full re-prep recommendation is justified by the compliance and new-class gains. The hard threshold is also the gate as defined. The real defect is reporting a knife-edge single-seed verdict with no uncertainty.

items.title: EMA starts at the warm-start weights, so early 'best' checkpoints are partly v1
items.claim: The EMA shadow starts at the initial weights (the v1 snap_60000 for the continuation arms) and has decay 0.9997, while evaluations happen every 5000 steps. At step 5000 the selected EMA weights still hold 0.9997^5000 = e^-1.5 ≈ 22% of the untouched v1 weights (≈ 5% at 10k, ≈ 1% at 15k). Selection over {5k, 10k, 15k} is therefore systematically biased toward the warm start, which was trained identity-only.
items.evidence: train3.py:248 `self.p = [p.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]` (initialised at init). g_cfg.sh: `ema=0.9997, eval_every=5000, steps=15000, init=.../snap_60000.pt`. train3.py:731/736: best.pt = EMA state at the lowest identity score. Observed: c_oh best.pt = 5k (identity 4.9% vs 5.1% at 15k; rotated 11.8% vs 6.8%), which is what a 22% v1 admixture produces.
items.consequence: best.pt of any continuation arm, which is also the checkpoint used by eval_views, evalnet and lat_full, can be a blend with the pre-arm model. This dilutes the arm effects that the views and the gate then measure. Switching to a multi-view score alone will not remove this bias.
items.fix: Use a bias-corrected EMA (divide by 1 - d^t, as Adam does, or start the EMA at the first post-warmup step), or exclude evaluations with d^t > 1% from best.pt selection. Evaluate more often than every 5k steps so that the selection has more than 3 candidates.

verification.reasoning: The EMA is built at train3.py:447, after the init checkpoint is loaded at lines 434-441, and EMA.__init__ copies the current parameters with no bias correction (line 248). With ema=0.9997 and eval_every=5000 (g_cfg.sh), the step-5k EMA holds 0.9997^5000 = e^-1.5 ≈ 22% of the snap_60000 weights, about 5% at 10k and about 1% at 15k. best.pt is the EMA state with the lowest identity score (lines 731-738), chosen from only 3 candidates. For c_oh this favours the identity-trained warm start, and it matches the observed choice of the 5k checkpoint over 15k. The effect is real and it biases selection toward the pre-arm model.

items.title: The selection score is identity-view, mean-based and, in step 1, energy-only, so it does not match what the gate measures
items.claim: train3 validates only the identity view (`g = s_.geo  # identity view`) and scores the mean energy excess + mean sensitivity + 0.5·p90, averaged over families. train1 (used for the r2 pilot arms) selects best.pt on the worst-class mean ENERGY only, with no sensitivity term. The gate is a max over 12 traction-consistent loads of compliance AND per-cell 8-corner sensitivity. In the pilot, the classes closest to the gate (force_c, glued) were excluded from selection ('5 个基础类选模').
items.evidence: train3.py:624 (identity only); train3.py:349-364 score(); train1.py:101 `score = max(v[c]['mean'] for v in ev.values() for c in v if sc is None or c in sc)`, train1.py:104 best on it. g_chain3.sh gates `$O/$a/best.pt`. Documented case: c_oh best = 5k, 2x worse on rotations than 15k.
items.consequence: The checkpoint that is gated and deployed can be worse on the gate (sensitivity) and on rotated geometries than other snapshots of the same run. The arm-to-arm gate differences (2.06 vs 2.97/3.00) partly reflect which of 5 snapshots an energy-only criterion picked, not the arm itself.
items.fix: For v2: a multi-view score (identity + fixed O_h views) that includes sensitivity (mean and p90) and the force_c/glued classes. For step-1-style arms, add the sensitivity term to train1's score, or gate every snapshot (snap_*.pt) and report both the gate of best.pt and the best gate over snapshots.

verification.reasoning: train3.py:624 validates only the identity view (g = s_.geo). score() (lines 349-364) is mean energy + mean sensitivity + 0.5·p90 over families, with no view and no max. train1.py:101 selects on the max over geometries/classes of the class-mean energy, with no sensitivity term, and the pilot restricted score_classes to the 5 base classes (doc section 8). The gate is a max over loads of compliance and per-cell 8-corner sensitivity. The mismatch is real, the c_oh 5k selection shows it matters, and chain3 gates only best.pt (train1 keeps no snapshots, so other checkpoints could not be gated after the fact anyway).

items.title: Non-finite validation results are silently dropped from the selection score, which rewards divergence
items.claim: families() aggregates per-geometry class means with _nanmean, which discards NaN/inf. A geometry on which the network diverges (e_hat inf/NaN) is removed from its family's mean instead of penalising it, so the score can go down. If a whole family becomes non-finite, score() drops that family too (line 364). If the very first score is NaN, `sc < best` is always False and best.pt is never updated again.
items.evidence: train3.py:327-330 `v = [x for x in v if x is not None and np.isfinite(x)]`; train3.py:342 `mean=_nanmean([r['mean'] for r in rs])`; train3.py:364 `return _nanmean([p['total'] for p in parts.values()])`; train3.py:736 `if best is None or sc < best`. eval_geo returns NaN/inf means whenever any sample's field is non-finite (bank samples are cleaned beforehand, so this can only come from the network). The trainer has NONFINITE_LOSS/NONFINITE_GRAD guards, so non-finite outputs are a known path.
items.consequence: A checkpoint that blows up on the hardest validation geometry can become best.pt, and then be gated and deployed. compare_arms' family tables inherit the same silent exclusion.
items.fix: Treat a non-finite per-geometry metric as +inf (or a large penalty) in families()/score(), log a VAL_NONFINITE event, and never select a checkpoint with any non-finite validation entry. Initialise best only from finite scores.

verification.reasoning: _nanmean (train3.py:327-330) drops None/NaN/inf. families() uses it for the per-family class means (line 342), so a geometry whose mean is inf or NaN silently leaves its family mean. score() drops a non-finite family total (line 364). If the first score is NaN, then best=NaN and 'sc < best' is never true, so best.pt freezes at that checkpoint (line 736). eval_geo takes plain e.mean(), so one non-finite sample makes the geometry mean non-finite. I downgraded it to minor because it is a latent path: no validation divergence has been observed, and training-side non-finite guards exist. The logic flaw itself is real.

items.title: evalnet always uses 0020 FULL as the neighbour, whatever the test cell's family
items.claim: The standing gate glues the cut test cell to ITS family FULL parent. evalnet hard-codes `FULL = 'fresh_train_0020_full'` for every case. LT.build glues by absolute node position and raises nothing when interface nodes do not match, so a test cell from another family is silently glued to a geometrically unrelated neighbour. evalnet also loads weights with strict=False and discards `missing`.
items.evidence: evalnet.py:16 `FULL = 'fresh_train_0020_full'`; evalnet.py:65 `lat = LT.build(case, FULL, conf, cfg['body'])`; lattice3.py:193-201 (keys by absolute position; unmatched nodes simply become separate DOFs); evalnet.py:55 `missing = model.load_state_dict(ck['model'], strict=False)`, never checked. By contrast, lat_full --custom and bench_deploy use family_full / the regex.
items.consequence: Any evalnet gate on a non-0020 cell (the v2 plan gates held-out families 'each with its own FULL parent') measures a different lattice, with partially free interfaces, and reports gate_pass with no warning. A checkpoint with renamed keys would be gated with random layers.
items.fix: Use DC.family_full(case) (or require an explicit --nbr) in evalnet. Assert that the fraction of test-cell interface port DOFs matched to neighbour DOFs is about 1. Use MD.load_compat (strict) or fail on non-empty missing_keys.

verification.reasoning: evalnet.py:16 hard-codes FULL='fresh_train_0020_full'. LT.build glues by absolute grid position with no matched-fraction check (lattice3.py:102-113), and load_state_dict(strict=False) discards the missing keys (line 55). However, every evalnet call in the scripts uses the checkpoint's default cases, and those are all step-1 0020-family cells (r1/r2/full), so no existing result is affected. A train3 checkpoint's cfg has no 'cases' key, so evalnet on a step-2 checkpoint fails loudly unless cases are passed explicitly. The held-out-family plan uses lat_full --custom, which falls back to DC.family_full. This is a latent footgun, not a current error, so I downgraded it to minor.

items.title: The deployment benchmark times the learned route with TF32 convolutions, the lossy precision that was rejected
items.claim: bench_deploy never disables cuDNN TF32, and neither it nor evalnet, lat_full or eval_views honours the checkpoint's cfg 'conv_fp32'. The chain3 invocation sets no OPL_CONV_FP32. All learned timings, energy ratios and the learned-lattice CG therefore run with TF32 conv3d, which the standing rules rejected as an acceleration. In that mode the written-out adjoint also gives a non-symmetric S_hat (up to 1.4e-3 asymmetry), which CG assumes away.
items.evidence: models.py: set_conv_fp32 only via env OPL_CONV_FP32=1 or trainer cfg (train1/train3 main); bench_deploy.py has no such call. g_fix3d.sh runs `bench_deploy.py $O/c_ctrl/best.pt ...` without the env. The V2 doc's learned Ŝq B=16 on FULL 0007 is 199 ms, which is exactly the TF32 number in the TF32 table (199 -> 213 ms fp32; r1: 38 -> 52 ms, +37%).
items.consequence: Learned-route speed is overstated by about 7% (FULL) to 37% (cut cells) relative to the admissible fp32 path. The learned lattice CG rows (Jacobi 2524 iterations vs exact 2149) mix operator quality with asymmetry effects. Deployment conclusions ('单方向 Ŝq 快 5×') are measured under a rejected precision mode.
items.fix: Have bench_deploy, evalnet, lat_full and eval_views call MD.set_conv_fp32(ck['cfg'].get('conv_fp32', True for deployment)), and record torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 in every output JSON. Re-time the learned route in fp32 before quoting deployment numbers.

verification.reasoning: bench_deploy (and evalnet, lat_full, eval_views) never call MD.set_conv_fp32, and no script sets OPL_CONV_FP32. So all learned timings run with cuDNN TF32 conv3d, and the quoted 199 ms Ŝq B=16 on FULL 0007 is the TF32 number. I downgraded it because: (a) no current config sets conv_fp32, so honouring the cfg would change nothing today; (b) TF32 was the untouched historical default that the models were trained and evaluated under, not an acceleration someone chose; (c) the doc's section 4 already lists the fp32 timings (199 -> 213 ms, 38 -> 52 ms) and the asymmetry. The residual defect is that the deployment table quotes TF32 numbers and the benchmark does not record the precision mode.

items.title: compare_arms mixes checkpoints: the rule uses the last EVAL, the views and the gate use best.pt
items.claim: last_eval() takes the LAST EVAL of train.log (15k) for the decision, while the rotated-view metrics merged into the same record come from views_<arm>.json, which chain3 computes on best.pt. The steps of the two are never checked against each other, or against the control's step. The checkpoint that is gated and deployed (best.pt) is not the one the rule judged.
items.evidence: compare_arms.py:14-22 `ev[-1]`. g_fix3b.sh: `c_oh:$O/c_oh/best.pt ... run views_$n $PY -u eval_views.py $ck`. compare_arms.py:69-73 merges views_* into r['views'] next to 'better'. For c_oh, best.pt = 5k while last EVAL = 15k (V2 doc table). No assertion that e['step'] == base['step'].
items.consequence: For c_oh, the compare record pairs the 15k identity rule result with 5k rotated metrics, so the conclusions drawn from one record come from two different models. An arm can be 'better' at its last step while its shipped best.pt is a different, earlier snapshot.
items.fix: Take the EVAL whose step equals the best.pt step (or evaluate both explicitly and label them). Store the checkpoint step inside views_*.json and assert that it matches. Assert equal steps between arm and control.

verification.reasoning: compare_arms.last_eval takes ev[-1] (lines 14-22). The views_* files come from eval_views run on best.pt (g_fix3b.sh). Neither file records or checks the step, and there is no assertion that the arm and control steps are equal. For c_oh, the record pairs the 15k identity rule result with 5k rotated metrics. I downgraded it because the V2 doc lists c_oh best (5k) and last (15k) as separate rows, so the reported conclusions did not actually conflate them. It is still a real tooling inconsistency between the checkpoint the rule judged and the one that is shipped.

items.title: O_h is adopted against the coded rule, on a metric the gate never measures
items.claim: Under the implemented rule, c_oh is 0/4 families with identity class ratios of about 1.25-1.40 (> 1.10), i.e. 'not better'. It is adopted for v2 on the rotated-view metric, which is not part of the rule or the gate. The gate (lattice3/evalnet/lat_full) only evaluates the cell in its own frame, and there on held-out identity-frame geometries the O_h model is about 30% worse.
items.evidence: V2 doc section 1: c_oh identity 4.9-5.1 / 5.8-5.9 / 3.4-3.8 vs control 3.9 / 4.6 / 2.7; '0/4 族'. compare_arms.py:68 threshold 1.10. There is no rotated-frame gate anywhere (LT.build has no view argument).
items.consequence: The v2 decision swaps the pre-registered criterion for a new one after seeing the data, and the new metric has no gate-level validation. If deployment cells are in-distribution orientations, v2 is expected to lose about 30% in identity energy error, which feeds straight into the gate compliance (≈ w·eps).
items.fix: Pre-register the multi-view criterion (weights for identity vs views) before the v2 run. Validate on the gate: lat_full on held-out families in the identity frame AND in rotated frames (rotate the whole two-cell lattice). Adopt O_h only if the identity-frame gate does not regress beyond noise.

verification.reasoning: O_h was never meant to be judged by the identity-view family rule. ARCH_REVIEW B6 introduces it because the user's standing scope says other orientations are covered by rotation augmentation ('你定的范围是"其他朝向靠旋转增广"'). It asks for the user's consent and pre-registers its own target: rotated error <= 1.2x unrotated, with the note that the identity-view gain is uncertain. So adopting it on the rotated metric is not a post-hoc swap of criteria. The identity cost (+30%) is stated openly, and v2 is marked provisional. The remaining valid point is that no gate-level (lattice) check covers either the identity regression or the rotated frames. Stage 5 plans a held-out-family lattice gate, which will measure the identity-frame effect.

items.title: Per-cell relative sensitivity error is ill-conditioned for cells carrying almost no energy; there is no floor in the code
items.claim: The per-cell 8-corner relative error divides by that cell's own sensitivity norm. For cells whose energy share w is about 0, the error is driven by the other cell's error transmitted through the interface, not by the cell itself. lat_full's gate_pass for the 'nbr'/'both' sets applies no energy-share floor, and the '≥1% share' number in the doc was computed outside the code.
items.evidence: lattice3.py:268 `vec = np.linalg.norm(s1 - s0, axis=1) / np.linalg.norm(s0, axis=1)`; lat_full.py:47 passes cmp_['gate_pass'] through unchanged. V2 doc section 7: r1+FULL y 'both' 43.8% vs 10.8% with a ≥1% floor; A7 161% at w=0.000. evalnet only records the test-cell share (lattice3.py:285).
items.consequence: The fully-learned (deployment) gate verdict and max can be dominated by a denominator artefact. Numbers with a floor are not reproducible from the tool output.
items.fix: Keep the standing gate as it is, but have lattice3.compare also emit sens errors normalised by max(|s_c|, floor·|s_lattice|), or masked by the energy share w_c ≥ 1%, together with w for every cell and load, so that the proposed floor metric is computed in code.

verification.reasoning: lattice3.py:268 divides each cell's 8-corner error by that cell's own sensitivity norm, with no floor. gate_pass and the max are therefore dominated by near-zero-share cells (the 161% and 43.8% cases). That is the standing gate definition, which the finding proposes to keep. Its claim that floor numbers are not reproducible from tool output is wrong for lat_full: summarize() stores w (cells x loads) and sens_vec_rel_err (cells x loads), so the ≥1% floor metric can be derived from the JSON. For evalnet, the neighbour's share is 1 minus the test cell's share. The only real gap is that the floored metric is not computed in code.

items.title: gate_pass ignores whether CG converged; the learned S_hat is not exactly symmetric
items.claim: Lattice.evaluate stops at maxit (300 by default, 400 from the callers) without failing, and it tests the recursive residual only. gate_pass never checks pcg_residual. With a non-symmetric learned operator (the autograd or written-out adjoint under TF32) CG has no convergence guarantee. The C_hat ≤ C bound checked in lat_full is also only approximate.
items.evidence: lattice3.py:241-258 (loop, `res['pcg_residual'] = ...` recorded only); lattice3.py:282 gate_pass has no residual term. In practice the ideal preconditioner converged in 13 iterations (bench), so no current result is known to be affected.
items.consequence: A poorly converged solve (a bad checkpoint with large mu, or a stronger asymmetry) would still be scored and could be reported as pass or fail without a flag.
items.fix: Set gate_pass = None (invalid) when pcg_residual > 1e-8 or when it = maxit. Optionally compute the true residual F - A X once at the end, and symmetrise the learned apply (0.5·(S_hat + S_hat^T) via one extra adjoint) inside the evaluator only.

verification.reasoning: Lattice.evaluate (lattice3.py:241-260) exits at maxit without an error and only records pcg_residual, which is the recursively updated residual. compare() (line 282) sets gate_pass without looking at the residual or the iteration count. With the ideal preconditioner, convergence takes about 13 iterations, so no current result is known to be affected. The missing validity flag is real.

items.title: LAT_SKIP_NBR_SENS silently removes the neighbour from gate_pass
items.claim: With LAT_SKIP_NBR_SENS set, the neighbour's sensitivities become NaN, and np.nanmax in compare() then computes gate_sens_max and gate_pass over the test cell only. The output still says 'gate_pass' with no flag, which contradicts the 'neighbour included' rule. Several historical gate runs used it (qcons.sh, q3r2b.sh, qre2.sh: LATTICE_cons.json / LATTICE_testsens.json).
items.evidence: lattice3.py:229-231; lattice3.py:280-282 `np.nanmax(vec[:, g])`. Only `sens_cells_measured` (line 281) reveals it.
items.consequence: Gate verdicts from those files are not the standing gate. Mixing them with the full gate files (LATTICE_cons_full.json) in comparisons can overstate passes.
items.fix: Set gate_pass = None (or 'partial') when sens_cells_measured < number of cells, and put the env setting into the output record.

verification.reasoning: With LAT_SKIP_NBR_SENS set, _measure_ fills the neighbour's sensitivities with NaN (lattice3.py:229-231). np.nanmax(vec[:, g]) then computes gate_sens_max and gate_pass over the test cell only (lines 280-282). Only sens_cells_measured reveals this, and the env setting is not recorded. The scripts use it for LATTICE_testsens.json and also for LATTICE_cons.json, whose name does not signal the partial gate. The damage is limited because a separate *_cons_full.json exists for those runs.

items.title: bench_deploy: single-shot timings with no warm-up, and learned setup costs missing from the reported table
items.claim: The factorisations (fp64 first, fp32 second) and the fastnet freeze are timed once, without warm-up, so the first cuDSS/Triton call includes library initialisation. The learned route's per-cell setup (netdata_s, geo_s, model_cache_s: MGCache, GP-face setup, geometry path) is recorded, but the V2 table lists only 'freeze 0.15 s' against the 3.4-8.6 s factorisation.
items.evidence: bench_deploy.py:116 `timed(lambda: C.factor(...))` (reps=1, warm=0); bench_deploy.py:126-131 netdata/geo/model_cache/freeze timed separately. V2 doc section 6 '分解 fp64 / fp32 | 8.6 s / 3.4 s | —（冻结 0.15 s）'.
items.consequence: The claimed per-cell saving of the learned route ('省分解 3–9 s') may be overstated: the fp64 factor may carry the first-call overhead, and the learned route's own setup is omitted.
items.fix: Warm up both routes once on a throwaway cell (or repeat per cell), and report the full per-cell cost of each route (learned: netdata + Geo + cache + freeze).

verification.reasoning: This is partly refuted. The factorisations are timed once with warm=0 (bench_deploy.py:116), but the doc's table quotes FULL 0007, the 4th cell on the command line (r2, r1, full, 0007). cuDSS and Triton were already initialised by the earlier cells, so the first-call overhead does not affect the quoted 8.6 s / 3.4 s. The omission is real: the learned route's own per-cell setup (netdata_s, geo_s, model_cache_s) is recorded (lines 126-129), but the doc table shows only 'freeze 0.15 s' against the factorisation cost.

items.title: The default gate cells are step-2 validation geometries, used both for selection and for the gate
items.claim: lat_full's default pairs (r2/r1 = 0020 cover01 cells) and evalnet's fixed 0020 neighbour both use family 0020. That family is a step-2 validation family (V2 doc section 7: '0020 r1/r2 是 step‑2 的 val 几何'), i.e. one of the 4 families that choose best.pt and decide the arms.
items.evidence: lat_full.py:103-104 spec from DC.R2/DC.R1; evalnet.py:16. V2 doc section 7 note.
items.consequence: The step-2 gate numbers are optimistically biased by selection on the same family. This is harmless now (they fail by a wide margin), but it would matter once v2 approaches the threshold.
items.fix: For step-2/v2, gate only on held-out (test/development) families with --custom and family_full, as the stage-5 plan states, and make the defaults refuse val-family cells for step-2 checkpoints.

verification.reasoning: lat_full's defaults (DC.R2/R1/FULL, all 0020) and evalnet's fixed 0020 neighbour make the default gate cells the 0020 family, and the doc confirms '0020 r1/r2 是 step-2 的 val 几何'. For step-2 checkpoints, the default gate therefore uses a family that took part in selection. The doc already discloses this. The defaults were designed for the step-1 pairs, and the step-2 numbers are far from the threshold, so the bias is harmless for now, as the finding itself says.
